73. McGraw-Hill Education

Textbooks are the primary vehicles by which students encounter and internalise the historical experiences of their nation and the world. As a major publisher of education materials in the United States, McGraw-Hill Education (hereafter MH) occupies a significant role in shaping how history is framed and taught. Yet, as several examples illustrate, the decisions made by MH in wording, framing, omission and emphasis have at times produced inaccurate or misleading representations of historical facts, raising concerns for educators, historians and parents.

One of the most widely discussed criticisms was the treatment of the transatlantic slave trade and slavery in America. In 2015 a mother in Pearland, Texas, flagged a caption in a MH 'World Geography' textbook that read: “The Atlantic Slave Trade between the 1500s and 1800s brought millions of workers from Africa to the southern United States to work on agricultural plantations."

This phrasing of enslaved Africans as 'workers' implied voluntary immigration, suggested labour was paid and minimised the forced nature and oppression of slavery. This in turn shapes student perceptions. MH subsequently acknowledged that the language “did not adequately convey that Africans were both forced into migration and to labor against their will as slaves.” Although the publisher updated the online version and offered corrective options for print copies, concerns lingered about remaining print editions and the delay of some replacements.

The Japanese government asked MH for the removal or revision of passages in one of their textbooks referencing so-called 'comfort women' which described the procurement of women for military brothels during World War II by the Japanese Imperial Army. MH refused to accede to the request. This episode, while not strictly a factual error, illustrates how textbook publishers are drawn into the contested terrain of national memory, narrative control and the selection of historical facts themselves. The push to revise the language highlights how respected publishers may be pressured from domestic or international actors regarding what version of history is told or omitted.

Historians argue that textbooks published by large firms, including MH, frequently suffer from deeper structural issues. As one analysis in The Atlantic observed: “The textbooks teachers rely on so heavily are prone to flaws … sometimes they are fundamental distortions of the contexts leading up to many of today’s most dire social ills.” In other words, inaccuracies may not solely consist of isolated typos or wrong dates but also the ways in which causes and consequences are presented, what is emphasised or omitted and how language choices encode ideological perspectives.

What is at stake extends beyond mere factual accuracy. Textbooks perform more than the transmission of dates and names: they shape civic identity, moral reflection and understandings of power and justice. When a textbook minimises slavery or the treatment of enslaved Africans, it implicitly downplays racial injustice, structures of oppression and the consequences for descendants. When another textbook becomes subject to governmental pressure to alter the narrative of its wartime role, the question of memory and accountability looms.

MH has defended its editorial process, stating that it engages with expert authors, consultants and educators and that it aims to 'minimise bias, reflect a balance of perspectives and include up-to-date scholarship.' Nonetheless, recurring controversies reveal that even major publishers are vulnerable to distortions, omissions, outdated language, or politically contested content. 

What problems arise from relying on one publisher to produce all textbooks for secondary or tertiary studies? Can we be sure we are getting accurate information? Do you see the potential for corruption when one company has most of the control? Are there parallels with Big Pharma and Montesanto? Cisco IOS XR Software for ASR 9000 Series Routers IPv4 Unicast Packets Denial of Service Vulnerability
https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-asr9k-tUyxcyXN?vs_f=Cisco%20Security%20Advisory%26vs_cat=Security%20Intelligence%26vs_type=RSS%26vs_p=Cisco%20IOS%20XR%20Software%20for%20ASR%209000%20Series%20Routers%20IPv4%20Unicast%20Packets%20Denial%20of%20Service%20Vulnerability%26vs_k=1

A vulnerability in the IPv4 packet processing functionality of Cisco IOS XR Software that affects Cisco ASR 9000 and 9900 Series Aggregation Services Routers as well as Cisco ASR 9902 and 9903 Compact High-Performance Routers could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to cause network processor (NP) errors, resulting in a line card reset or shutdown and a denial of service (DoS) condition. 
This vulnerability is due to the incorrect handling of crafted IPv4 packets that are received on an affected line card interface and processed as for-us traffic. The issue can result in an NP reset, causing traffic loss on the affected line card while it recovers. Under repeated reset conditions, the network processor may enter a persistent shutdown state, in which case an explicit line card reload may be required to restore traffic.
The vulnerability is within the IPv4 packet-processing path. Transit IPv4 traffic does not trigger this issue and IPv6 traffic cannot trigger it.

Cisco has released software updates that address this vulnerability. There are no workarounds that address this vulnerability.
This advisory is available at the following link:
https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-asr9k-tUyxcyXN
         
             Security Impact Rating:  High
